# Results — Study 467 (Bump-and-Run Reversal)

*Generated by [`examples/verify.py`](../examples/verify.py). The believers' claim — **a gentle
lead-in trendline, a speculative bump, then a break back below the trendline forecasts a
downward reversal: short the break** (Bulkowski) — encoded as a mechanical rule. The lead-in is
a least-squares trendline fit on a trailing window (slope gently positive); a bump is confirmed
when the close surges to ≥ 2× the lead-in's above-line height; a **short** fires on the first
close that *downcrosses* the extended lead-in line after a recent bump, entered at the **next
close** (one documented lag), and we measure the forward 5/10/20/60-day return of the short.
Offline & deterministic once cached; run `python examples/verify.py` to reproduce every number.*

## Data stamp

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Real tape | yfinance daily adjusted (**total-return**) closes for **SPY, QQQ, IWM, DIA, GLD** (public, no key) |
| Window | 2005-01-03 → 2026-05-29 (**As-of 2026-05-31**, partial June dropped; **21.4** years) |
| SPY fingerprint | `4cb5244f3990` (sha1[:12] of the close column, As-of slice) |
| Entries | **162** mechanical bump-and-run trendline-break shorts pooled across the 5 tapes (lead = 60, bump = 30, bump_mult = 2.0) |
| Timing / costs | lead-in fit on trailing bars only; bump confirmed on bars ≤ *t*; **short** on the first close below the line; enter the **next close** (one lag); hold 5/10/20/60 days; **1 bp** one-way × 2 legs per break |

> **Price-only vs total-return.** The ETFs are auto-adjusted (dividends reinvested) — labelled
> total-return everywhere. The Signal axis uses a basket of **surviving** liquid ETFs; this is a
> single-instrument pattern study, not a cross-sectional anomaly, so survivorship affects only
> the drift baseline (which is exactly what the random-entry control neutralizes). A short on an
> upward-drifting, dividend-paying index pays the drift away — the random short baseline carries
> that same headwind, so the comparison is fair.

## The signal — BARR-break short vs a drift-matched random short baseline (the honest test)

One-sample *t* is the **misleading** number (a short on a rising index loses by construction —
that is negative beta, not a dead rule); the **Welch break-vs-random** *t* is the test that
matters. Δ = break − random.

| horizon | n | break short | win% | one-sample *t* | random short | Δ (break−random) | net of cost | Welch *t* | *p* |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| 5-day  | 162 | −15.8 bps | 46% | −1.01 | +45.1 bps | **−60.9 bps** | −17.8 bps | −2.50 | 0.013 |
| 10-day | 162 | −23.1 bps | 46% | −0.86 | +48.1 bps | **−71.2 bps** | −25.1 bps | −2.00 | 0.046 |
| 20-day | 162 | −66.0 bps | 37% | −1.84 | +58.0 bps | **−123.9 bps** | −68.0 bps | −2.54 | 0.011 |
| 60-day | 162 | −253.0 bps | 36% | −4.09 | −121.1 bps | **−131.8 bps** | −255.0 bps | −1.72 | 0.085 |

Read it carefully. The bump-and-run break short **loses money** at every horizon (−16/−23/−66/−253
bps) — but that is mostly negative beta: shorting a drifting index. The decisive number is the
comparison to a **drift-matched random short**, and there the break short does **even worse**:
Δ = −61 / −71 / −124 / −132 bps, with the Welch break-vs-random *t* **negative and clearing −2 at
3 of 4 horizons** (−2.50 at 5d, −2.54 at 20d). In plain terms, **price tends to keep *rising*
after the bump-and-run break — the opposite of the forecast**. The pattern does not forecast a
reversal; if anything it marks a spot you'd least want to be short.

## Per-ticker (H = 20) — the break short loses to a random short everywhere

| ticker | entries | break short | one-sample *t* | random short | Δ (break−random) |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| SPY | 41 | −28.8 bps | −0.37 | +46.6 bps | **−75.3 bps** |
| QQQ | 38 | −25.9 bps | −0.30 | +24.2 bps | **−50.1 bps** |
| IWM | 25 | −138.6 bps | −1.44 | +138.2 bps | **−276.8 bps** |
| DIA | 41 | −33.9 bps | −0.75 | +55.1 bps | **−89.0 bps** |
| GLD | 17 | −215.7 bps | −2.18 | +25.8 bps | **−241.5 bps** |

The break-minus-random delta is **negative in all 5 names** — there is no instrument where the
bump-and-run break short beats a coin-flip short. A forecasting reversal pattern would show
positive deltas; this shows the reverse, consistently.

## Geometry placebo — scramble the shape, nothing changes

The decisive "does the bump-and-run geometry matter?" test: permute the per-bar log-returns
(keeping the price **marginal** but destroying the lead-in/bump/break *ordering*), rebuild the
entries, and compare. If the specific bump-and-run shape carried information, the scramble would
collapse the result.

| test | observed break-short 20d return | placebo *p* | draws |
|---|--:|--:|--:|
| SPY shuffled-window break | −28.8 bps | **0.359** | 500 |

**36% of scrambled-geometry tapes match or beat the real break short** (*p* = 0.359). The
bump-and-run shape carries no information — order-destroyed nonsense does just as well. "The
bump-then-break forecasts a reversal" is busted.

## Synthetic positive control — the harness CAN bank a real reversal

On a deterministic tape with a *planted* post-bump reversal (knob `edge`), the same break-short
rule behaves exactly as it must — so the flat/negative real-tape result is a genuine "nothing
there", not a dead detector.

| planted edge | n | break short | win% | one-sample *t* |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| **0.00** (no reversal) | 23 | +86.0 bps | 61% | +1.86 |
| **0.70** (real planted reversal) | 16 | +182.5 bps | 69% | **+3.45** |

With no planted reversal the control stays **below the *t* = 2 bar** (no false positive); a real
planted reversal lights up at *t* = +3.45 with a 69% win-rate. The detector is live and *can*
bank a genuine bump-and-run reversal — the real tape simply has none to bank.

## Verdict

- **Signal — NONE.** The bump-and-run break short does **not** beat a drift-matched random short;
  it does **significantly worse** (Δ = −61 / −71 / −124 / −132 bps at 5/10/20/60 days; Welch *t*
  = −2.50 / −2.00 / −2.54 / −1.72). The break does not forecast a fall — price tends to keep
  rising after it. The big one-sample *t* at 60d (−4.09) is just the negative beta of a short.
- **Tradability — MIRAGE.** There is no edge to deploy: the short loses in absolute terms (beta)
  *and* loses to a random short (no residual skill), and costs only deepen the hole. Nothing to
  scale.
- **"Does the bump-then-break forecast a reversal?" — BUSTED.** The shuffled-window placebo
  leaves the result intact (*p* = 0.359): order-scrambled nonsense does as well as the real
  bump-and-run shape, so the specific lead-in / bump / break geometry carries no forecasting
  information. The pattern is a descriptive after-the-fact label, not a reversal forecast.
